explanation: Subsection 2.8.3 notes that drivers making over-the-shoulder checks, most easily seen in motorcyclists and bicyclists, may be about to change lanes.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.8.3 - Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: According to subsection 2.8.3, when are you "in conflict" with another road user?
choice_a: When you have to change speed and/or direction to avoid hitting someone
choice_b: Whenever you are stopped at a red light
choice_c: Only when a collision has actually occurred
choice_d: Whenever another vehicle is in an adjacent lane
explanation: Subsection 2.8.3 defines being in conflict as having to change speed and/or direction to avoid hitting someone, occurring at intersections, merges, and lane changes.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.8.3 - Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: According to subsection 2.8.4, why should you look for hazards and think about the emergencies that could develop?
choice_a: To pass the CDL knowledge test only
choice_b: To have time to plan a way out of any emergency
choice_c: To reduce fuel consumption
choice_d: Because it is a legal requirement to narrate hazards aloud
explanation: Subsection 2.8.4 explains that you look for hazards so you have time to plan a way out of any emergency that could develop.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.8.4 - Always Have a Plan

question: What clues might indicate a driver is a confused tourist, according to subsection 2.8.3?
choice_a: A clean windshield and working turn signals
choice_b: Driving exactly at the speed limit
choice_c: Car-top luggage and out-of-state license plates
choice_d: A commercial vehicle logo on the door
explanation: Subsection 2.8.3 lists car-top luggage and out-of-state license plates as clues to tourists unfamiliar with the area, who can be hazardous.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.8.3 - Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: What behavior does the manual describe as typical of "drivers in a hurry" around commercial vehicles?
choice_a: They always maintain a large following gap
choice_b: They wait patiently behind slow trucks
choice_c: They flash their headlights politely before passing
choice_d: They may pass without a safe gap in oncoming traffic, cutting too close in front of you
explanation: Subsection 2.8.3 notes drivers in a hurry may pass without a safe gap in oncoming traffic, cutting too close in front of you, or pull in front of you to avoid being stuck behind you.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.8.3 - Drivers Who Are Hazards

question: How does subsection 2.9 define a driver distraction?
choice_a: Anything that takes your attention away from driving
choice_b: Only cell phone use while driving
choice_c: Any activity performed while the vehicle is stopped
choice_d: A malfunction in the vehicle's electronics
explanation: Subsection 2.9 defines a driver distraction as anything that takes your attention away from driving.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9 - Distracted Driving

question: According to the Large Truck Crash Causation Study (LTCCS) cited in the manual, what percentage of large-truck crashes occurred when the CMV driver was externally distracted?
choice_a: 2 percent
choice_b: 8 percent
choice_c: 15 percent
choice_d: 23 percent
explanation: Subsection 2.9.1 states the LTCCS reported 8 percent of large-truck crashes occurred when drivers were externally distracted, and 2 percent when internally distracted.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.1 - The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: According to research cited in subsection 2.9.2/2.9.3, talking on a cell phone (even hands-free) saps the brain of what percentage of the energy it would normally devote to safe driving?
choice_a: 8 percent
choice_b: 15 percent
choice_c: 39 percent
choice_d: 60 percent
explanation: Subsection 2.9 states research indicates the burden of talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of 39% of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.1 - The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: The manual describes physical, mental, and what combined type of distraction as being especially dangerous?
choice_a: Emotional and financial distraction
choice_b: Auditory and olfactory distraction
choice_c: Environmental distraction
choice_d: Both physical and mental distraction, such as texting or talking on a cell phone
explanation: Subsection 2.9.3 identifies physical distraction, mental distraction, and combined physical-and-mental distraction (like texting or phone use) as the three types, with the combined type being most dangerous.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.3 - Types of Distractions

question: After how many convictions for hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV will your CDL be disqualified?
choice_a: Two or more
choice_b: One
choice_c: Five
choice_d: Ten
explanation: Subsection 2.9.4 states your CDL will be disqualified after two or more convictions of any state law on hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.4 - Cell/Mobile Phones

question: What is the maximum civil penalty a driver can face for violating the hand-held mobile telephone restriction, according to the manual?
choice_b: Up to $2,750
explanation: Subsection 2.9.4 states civil penalties on drivers for violating the hand-held phone prohibition can be up to $2,750.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.4 - Cell/Mobile Phones

question: What is the maximum civil penalty an employer/motor carrier can face for allowing a driver to use a hand-held phone, per the manual?
explanation: Subsection 2.9.4 states employers may be subject to civil penalties of up to $11,000 for allowing or requiring hand-held phone use.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.4 - Cell/Mobile Phones

question: What is the emergency exception to the hand-held mobile phone restriction?
choice_a: There is no exception under any circumstance
choice_b: An exception only for weather emergencies
choice_c: An exception only during daylight hours
choice_d: It allows use of a hand-held phone if necessary to communicate with law enforcement or other emergency services
explanation: Subsection 2.9.4 states there is an emergency exception allowing drivers to use hand-held phones if necessary to communicate with law enforcement officials or other emergency services.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.4 - Cell/Mobile Phones

question: How much greater are the odds of a safety-critical event for CMV drivers who dial a mobile phone while driving, compared to those who don't?
choice_a: 6 times greater
choice_b: 2 times greater
choice_c: 10 times greater
choice_d: 23.2 times greater
explanation: Subsection 2.9.4 states research shows dialing a mobile phone while driving makes the odds of a safety-critical event 6 times greater for CMV drivers.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.4 - Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Dialing drivers took their eyes off the road for an average of 3.8 seconds. At 55 mph, how far does this equate to?
choice_a: 61 feet
choice_b: 306 feet, about the length of a football field
choice_c: 419 feet
choice_d: 100 feet
explanation: Subsection 2.9.4 states 3.8 seconds at 55 mph (80.7 feet per second) equates to about 306 feet traveled without looking at the road, roughly a football field's length.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.4 - Cell/Mobile Phones

question: How much greater are the odds of a safety-critical event for CMV drivers who text while driving, compared to those who don't?
choice_a: 6 times greater
choice_b: 15 times greater
choice_c: 23.2 times greater
choice_d: 39 times greater
explanation: Subsection 2.9.5 states research shows texting while driving makes the odds of a safety-critical event 23.2 times greater for CMV drivers.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.5 - Texting

question: Sending or receiving a text takes a driver's eyes off the road for an average of 4.6 seconds. At 55 mph, about how far does the vehicle travel during that time?
choice_a: 216 feet
choice_b: 142 feet
choice_c: 61 feet
choice_d: 371 feet, the length of a football field
explanation: Subsection 2.9.5 states 4.6 seconds at 55 mph equates to about 371 feet, roughly the length of a football field, traveled without looking at the road.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.5 - Texting

question: How long is the CDL disqualification for a second texting-while-driving conviction within 3 years, according to the manual?
choice_a: 60 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_c: 90 days
choice_d: 120 days
explanation: Subsection 2.9.5 states disqualification is 60 days for the second offense within 3 years and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.5 - Texting

question: Which of the following is a tip the manual gives to avoid becoming a distracted driver?
choice_a: Program your GPS and select radio stations while driving in light traffic
choice_b: Review maps, program the GPS, and plan your route before you begin driving
choice_c: Read text messages only at red lights
choice_d: Keep unnecessary objects loose in the vehicle for quick access
explanation: Subsection 2.9.6 advises reviewing maps, programming the GPS, and planning your route before you begin driving, not while driving.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.6 - Don't Drive Distracted

question: According to subsection 2.9.6, what happens to crash rates if drivers react half a second slower because of distractions?
choice_a: Crashes decrease slightly
choice_b: Crash rates stay the same
choice_c: Crashes double
choice_d: Crashes increase by 10 percent
explanation: Subsection 2.9.6 states that if drivers react a half-second slower because of distractions, crashes double.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.6 - Don't Drive Distracted

question: What should you do when you notice another driver appears distracted, according to subsection 2.9.7?
choice_a: Pass them as quickly as possible to get away
choice_b: Flash your high beams to alert them
choice_c: Tailgate closely to get their attention
choice_d: Give the distracted driver plenty of room and maintain your safe following distance
explanation: Subsection 2.9.7 advises giving a distracted driver plenty of room and maintaining a safe following distance, being careful when passing them.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.9.7 - Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers

question: How does the manual define "aggressive driving"?
choice_a: Operating a motor vehicle in a selfish, bold, or pushy manner, without regard for the rights or safety of others
choice_b: Any driving above the posted speed limit
choice_c: Operating a vehicle with intent to physically harm another driver
choice_d: Driving while using a hand-held phone
explanation: Subsection 2.10.1 defines aggressive driving as operating a motor vehicle in a selfish, bold, or pushy manner without regard for the rights or safety of others.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.1 - What Is It?

question: How does the manual define "road rage"?
choice_a: Excessive honking of the horn
choice_b: Operating a vehicle with the intent of doing harm to others or physically assaulting a driver or their vehicle
choice_c: Driving faster than 10 mph over the limit
choice_d: Refusing to use a turn signal
explanation: Subsection 2.10.1 defines road rage as operating a motor vehicle with the intent of doing harm to others or physically assaulting a driver or their vehicle.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.1 - What Is It?

question: What tip does the manual give for reducing driving stress?
choice_a: Drive faster to shorten trip time
choice_b: Avoid taking breaks during long trips
choice_c: Listen to "easy listening" music and give the drive your full attention
choice_d: Argue back if another driver is aggressive
explanation: Subsection 2.10.2 suggests reducing stress by listening to "easy listening" music and giving the drive your full attention rather than becoming distracted.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.2 - Don't Be an Aggressive Driver

question: What does the manual advise about gestures while driving?
choice_a: Use hand gestures to communicate with other drivers instead of signals
choice_b: Wave to apologize for mistakes
choice_c: Gesturing is fine as long as one hand stays on the wheel
choice_d: Avoid any gestures, even seemingly harmless ones like shaking your head, that might anger another driver
explanation: Subsection 2.10.2 advises avoiding gestures that might anger another driver, even seemingly harmless expressions of irritation.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.2 - Don't Be an Aggressive Driver

question: What attitude does subsection 2.10.2 recommend if another driver seems eager to get in front of you?
choice_a: Be cautious and courteous, saying "Be my guest" to yourself to avoid feeling offended
choice_b: Block them from merging
choice_c: Speed up to prevent them from passing
choice_d: Flash your high beams repeatedly
explanation: Subsection 2.10.2 suggests being a cautious and courteous driver, mentally saying "Be my guest," which becomes a habit that reduces offense at other drivers' actions.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.2 - Don't Be an Aggressive Driver

question: What is the first and foremost thing the manual advises you do when confronted by an aggressive driver?
choice_a: Speed up to get away as fast as possible
choice_b: Make every attempt to get out of their way
choice_c: Pull over and confront them
choice_d: Flash your lights to warn them off
explanation: Subsection 2.10.3 states the first and foremost response is to make every attempt to get out of the aggressive driver's way.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.3 - What You Should Do When Confronted by an Aggressive Driver

question: According to subsection 2.10.3, what should you do regarding eye contact with an aggressive driver?
choice_a: Maintain steady eye contact to show confidence
choice_b: Stare them down until they back off
choice_c: Avoid eye contact
choice_d: Make eye contact only through your mirrors
explanation: Subsection 2.10.3 advises avoiding eye contact with an aggressive driver.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.3 - What You Should Do When Confronted by an Aggressive Driver

question: What information should you provide when reporting an aggressive driver to authorities?
choice_a: Only the time of day
choice_b: Nothing; aggressive driving cannot be reported
choice_c: Your own insurance information
choice_d: Vehicle description, license number, location, and direction of travel if possible
explanation: Subsection 2.10.3 instructs drivers reporting aggressive drivers to provide a vehicle description, license number, location, and direction of travel, if possible.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.3 - What You Should Do When Confronted by an Aggressive Driver

question: If an aggressive driver becomes involved in a crash farther down the road, what should you do?
choice_a: Stop a safe distance from the crash scene, wait for police, and report the behavior you witnessed
choice_b: Drive past quickly without stopping
choice_c: Pull the driver from the wreck yourself
choice_d: Ignore the crash and continue your route
explanation: Subsection 2.10.3 advises stopping a safe distance from the crash scene, waiting for police to arrive, and reporting the driving behavior you witnessed.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.3 - What You Should Do When Confronted by an Aggressive Driver

question: What does subsection 2.10.3 mean by "put your pride in the back seat" when confronted by an aggressive driver?
choice_a: Physically move to the back seat for safety
choice_b: Do not challenge the aggressive driver by speeding up or trying to hold your own in your lane
choice_c: Apologize to the other driver over the radio
choice_d: Let a passenger take over driving
explanation: Subsection 2.10.3 instructs drivers not to challenge an aggressive driver by speeding up or attempting to hold their own in the travel lane.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.10.3 - What You Should Do When Confronted by an Aggressive Driver

question: According to subsection 2.11.1, why are drivers at greater risk at night?
choice_a: Traffic volume is always higher at night
choice_b: Speed limits increase after dark
choice_c: Drivers can't see hazards as quickly as in daylight, so they have less time to respond
choice_d: Headlights are prohibited on rural roads
explanation: Subsection 2.11.1 explains drivers can't see hazards as quickly at night as in daylight, giving them less time to respond and avoid a crash.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.1 - It's More Dangerous

question: What does the manual say about wearing dark or tinted corrective lenses at night?
choice_a: They are recommended to reduce glare
choice_b: They are required by law in some states
choice_c: They have no effect on night vision
choice_d: They should be avoided, since they cut down the light needed to see clearly at night
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 advises avoiding dark or tinted corrective lenses at night because they cut down the light you need to see clearly under night driving conditions.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: How long can it take to recover from glare blindness, and why is this dangerous?
choice_a: Several seconds; even two seconds of glare blindness can be dangerous since a vehicle at 55 mph travels over half a football field's length in that time
choice_b: Several minutes; but there is no real danger
choice_c: Under one second; it has no real effect
choice_d: Glare has no measurable recovery time
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 states it can take several seconds to recover from glare, and even two seconds of glare blindness is dangerous because a vehicle going 55 mph travels more than half the length of a football field during that time.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: According to NHTSA estimates cited in the manual, about how many police-reported crashes a year result from drowsy driving?
choice_d: 1 million
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 states NHTSA estimates 100,000 police-reported crashes a year are the result of drowsy driving.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: According to the National Sleep Foundation poll cited in the manual, what percentage of Americans admit to actually having fallen asleep at the wheel?
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 cites the National Sleep Foundation's poll finding 36% of Americans admit to having fallen asleep at the wheel.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: Which group does research cited in subsection 2.11.2 identify as being at increased risk for fall-asleep crashes?
choice_a: Drivers under age 21 exclusively
choice_b: Only drivers who work a single job
choice_c: Drivers who never drive at night
choice_d: Young males, shift workers, commercial drivers (especially long-haul), and those with untreated sleep disorders
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 identifies young males, shift workers, commercial drivers (especially long-haul), and people with untreated or chronic sleep deprivation as at increased risk for fall-asleep crashes.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: According to the manual, at least what percentage of all heavy truck crashes involve fatigue?
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 states at least 15% of all heavy truck crashes involve fatigue.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: A congressionally mandated study of 80 long-haul truck drivers found that drivers averaged how much sleep per day?
choice_a: 8 hours
choice_b: Less than 5 hours
choice_c: 6 to 7 hours
choice_d: More than 9 hours
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 cites a study finding 80 long-haul truck drivers averaged less than 5 hours of sleep per day (FMCSA, 1996).
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: According to the NTSB report cited in the manual, drowsy driving was probably the cause of what?
choice_a: One-quarter of all truck accidents
choice_b: All nighttime accidents
choice_c: More than half of crashes leading to a truck driver's death
choice_d: Fewer than 5% of fatal truck crashes
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 states the NTSB (1990) reported drowsy driving was probably the cause of more than half of crashes leading to a truck driver's death.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: According to subsection 2.11.2, sleeping how many hours or less triples your risk of a fatigue-related crash?
choice_a: 8 hours
choice_b: 4 hours
choice_c: 3 hours
choice_d: 6 hours
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 ("Are You At Risk?") states that being sleep-deprived or fatigued with 6 hours of sleep or less triples your risk.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: According to the manual, working more than 60 hours a week increases your fatigue-related crash risk by what percentage?
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 states working more than 60 hours a week increases your risk of a fatigue-related crash by 40%.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: How many hours of sleep does the manual say adults need to maintain alertness?
choice_a: 5 to 6 hours
choice_b: 8 to 9 hours
choice_c: 10 to 12 hours
choice_d: 4 to 5 hours
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 ("Preventing drowsiness before a trip") states adults need 8 to 9 hours of sleep to maintain alertness.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: According to subsection 2.11.2, about how often should you take periodic breaks during long trips to maintain alertness?
choice_a: Every 500 miles or 8 hours
choice_b: Every 25 miles or 30 minutes
choice_c: About every 100 miles or 2 hours
choice_d: Only once per day
explanation: Subsection 2.11.2 recommends taking periodic breaks about every 100 miles or 2 hours during long trips.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.2 - Driver Factors

question: According to subsection 2.11.4, about how far can you see ahead with low beams versus high beams?
choice_a: Low beams 500 feet, high beams 250 feet
choice_b: Low beams 100 feet, high beams 200 feet
choice_c: Low beams 350 feet, high beams 500 feet
choice_d: Low beams about 250 feet, high beams about 350-500 feet
explanation: Subsection 2.11.4 states that with low beams you can see ahead about 250 feet, and with high beams about 350-500 feet.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.4 - Vehicle Factors

question: Within how many feet of an oncoming or followed vehicle should you dim your headlights, according to subsection 2.11.5?
choice_a: 500 feet
choice_b: 100 feet
choice_c: 1,000 feet
choice_d: 250 feet
explanation: Subsection 2.11.5 instructs drivers to dim their lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when following another vehicle within 500 feet.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.5 - Night Driving Procedures

question: What should you do to avoid glare from an oncoming vehicle's headlights, per subsection 2.11.5?
choice_a: Look directly at the oncoming headlights to judge distance
choice_b: Look slightly to the right at the right lane or edge marking, if available
choice_c: Close your eyes briefly
choice_d: Flash your own high beams back at them
explanation: Subsection 2.11.5 advises not looking directly at oncoming headlights, but looking slightly to the right at a right lane or edge marking, and not retaliating with high beams.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.11.5 - Night Driving Procedures

question: What is the best advice the manual gives for driving in fog?
choice_a: Use your high beams to see farther
choice_b: Drive at normal highway speed to clear the fog quickly
choice_c: Don't drive in fog; pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility improves
choice_d: Follow closely behind another vehicle's taillights
explanation: Subsection 2.12 states the best advice for driving in fog is "don't"—it's preferable to pull off the road until visibility is better.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12 - Driving in Fog

question: What type of headlights should you use when driving in fog, according to the manual?
choice_a: High beams for maximum visibility
choice_b: Parking lights only
choice_c: No lights, to avoid glare
choice_d: Low-beam headlights and fog lights
explanation: Subsection 2.12 instructs drivers to use low-beam headlights and fog lights for the best visibility in fog, even in daytime.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12 - Driving in Fog

question: What should you turn on while driving in fog, per subsection 2.12?
choice_a: Your 4-way flashers, to give vehicles behind a quicker chance to notice you
choice_b: Your interior dome light
choice_c: Your reverse lights
choice_d: Nothing additional beyond headlights
explanation: Subsection 2.12 advises turning on 4-way flashers in fog to give approaching vehicles from behind a quicker opportunity to notice your vehicle.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12 - Driving in Fog

question: Why does the manual caution against relying on taillights or headlights seen ahead in fog to know where the road is?
choice_a: Other vehicles' lights are always brighter than expected
choice_b: The vehicle you see may not actually be on the road at all
choice_c: Fog makes all lights appear the same color
choice_d: It is illegal to look at other vehicles' lights in fog
explanation: Subsection 2.12 warns that seeing taillights or headlights in front of you in fog may not truly indicate where the road is, since the vehicle may not be on the road at all.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12 - Driving in Fog

question: What assumption does the manual warn against making when you first enter fog?
choice_a: That fog will worsen as you continue
choice_b: That other drivers have their lights on
choice_c: That the fog will thin out after you enter it
choice_d: That fog only occurs at night
explanation: Subsection 2.12 states you should not assume the fog will thin out after you enter it, and should watch for foggy conditions and be ready to reduce speed.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12 - Driving in Fog

question: According to subsection 2.12, what should you avoid doing while driving through fog?
choice_a: Using your 4-way flashers
choice_b: Using low-beam headlights
choice_c: Watching for vehicles on the side of the road
choice_d: Passing other vehicles
explanation: Subsection 2.12 advises drivers to avoid passing other vehicles while driving in fog.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12 - Driving in Fog

question: According to the manual, should you stop along the side of the road while driving in fog?
choice_a: No, don't stop along the side of the road unless absolutely necessary
choice_b: Yes, always stop immediately upon entering fog
choice_c: Yes, but only on the left shoulder
choice_d: It doesn't matter, as long as flashers are on
explanation: Subsection 2.12 advises against stopping along the side of the road in fog unless absolutely necessary.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12 - Driving in Fog

question: What can you use as guides to determine how the road may curve ahead of you in fog?
choice_a: Other vehicles' brake lights
choice_b: Roadside highway reflectors
choice_c: Cell phone GPS exclusively
choice_d: The centerline paint color
explanation: Subsection 2.12 suggests using roadside highway reflectors as guides to determine how the road may curve ahead in foggy conditions.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.12 - Driving in Fog

question: Why should you make sure defrosters and heating equipment work before driving in winter, per subsection 2.13.1?
choice_a: They are only needed for passenger comfort
choice_b: State law requires functioning heaters, unrelated to safety
choice_c: They are needed for safe driving, along with checking that you know how to operate them
choice_d: They prevent tire chains from icing up
explanation: Subsection 2.13.1 states defrosters and heaters are needed for safe driving and you should make sure you know how to operate them.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: What should you use in the windshield washer reservoir in winter to prevent freezing of the fluid?
choice_a: Plain tap water
choice_b: Engine coolant
choice_c: Diesel exhaust fluid
choice_d: Windshield washer antifreeze
explanation: Subsection 2.13.1 recommends using windshield washer antifreeze to prevent the washer liquid from freezing.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: In winter conditions, what minimum tread depth does the manual specify for front tires?
choice_a: At least 4/32 inch in every major groove
choice_b: At least 6/32 inch
choice_c: At least 1/32 inch
choice_d: At least 8/32 inch
explanation: Subsection 2.13.1 reiterates you must have at least 4/32 inch tread depth on front tires (and at least 2/32 inch on other tires), and states more is better for winter driving.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: What does the manual advise regarding tire chains before winter driving conditions arise?
choice_a: Chains are illegal on commercial vehicles
choice_b: Learn how to put the chains on before you need to do it in snow and ice
choice_c: Only carry chains if crossing state lines
choice_d: Chains should be installed only by a mechanic
explanation: Subsection 2.13.1 advises learning how to put tire chains on before you actually need to do it in snow and ice, and checking them for broken hooks or links.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: Why are exhaust system leaks especially dangerous in winter, according to subsection 2.13.1?
choice_a: Cold exhaust corrodes the muffler faster
choice_b: They cause the engine to stall in snow
choice_c: Cab ventilation may be poor (windows rolled up), allowing poisonous carbon monoxide to leak in and cause drowsiness or death
choice_d: They reduce heater efficiency
explanation: Subsection 2.13.1 warns that exhaust leaks are especially dangerous when cab ventilation is poor, since carbon monoxide can cause sleepiness and, in large amounts, kill you.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: What does subsection 2.13.2 advise if the road is very slippery?
choice_a: Continue driving but reduce speed by half
choice_b: Use the engine brake or retarder to control speed
choice_c: Increase following distance only
choice_d: You shouldn't drive at all; stop at the first safe place
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 states if it is very slippery, you shouldn't drive at all and should stop at the first safe place.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: What clue can indicate ice has formed on the road, according to subsection 2.13.2?
choice_a: A lack of spray from other vehicles' tires
choice_b: Increased engine noise
choice_c: A drop in tire pressure warning light
choice_d: The windshield wipers turning on automatically
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 notes that a lack of spray from other vehicles indicates ice has formed on the road.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: Why does subsection 2.13.2 advise against using the engine brake or speed retarder on slippery roads?
choice_a: They increase fuel consumption
choice_b: They can cause the driving wheels to skid on slippery surfaces
choice_c: They are illegal in winter weather
choice_d: They wear out the clutch faster
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 advises not using the engine brake or speed retarder on slippery surfaces because they can cause the driving wheels to skid.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: What does subsection 2.13.2 advise about braking while taking curves on slippery winter roads?
choice_a: Brake gently throughout the curve for control
choice_b: Brake hard before entering to reduce speed quickly
choice_c: Take curves at slower speeds and don't brake while in the curve
choice_d: Braking in curves is unaffected by winter conditions
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 advises taking curves at slower speeds and not braking while in curves during winter driving.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: According to subsection 2.13.2, what happens to slipperiness as the temperature rises to the point where ice begins to melt?
choice_a: The road becomes less slippery
choice_b: There is no change in slipperiness
choice_c: Only bridges become more slippery
choice_d: The road becomes even more slippery
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 notes that as temperature rises toward the point where ice begins to melt, the road becomes even more slippery, so you should slow down more.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: What space-related adjustment does subsection 2.13.2 recommend for winter driving?
choice_a: Don't drive alongside other vehicles and keep a longer following distance
choice_b: Drive as close as possible to other vehicles for warmth
choice_c: Reduce following distance to save time
choice_d: Ignore traffic jams ahead since they clear quickly
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 advises not driving alongside other vehicles and keeping a longer following distance in winter conditions.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: What does subsection 2.13.2 advise regarding snowplows, salt trucks, and sand trucks?
choice_a: Pass them quickly to avoid delay
choice_b: Watch for them and give them plenty of room
choice_c: Follow closely to benefit from their cleared path
choice_d: They should always be reported to authorities
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 instructs drivers to watch for snowplows, salt trucks, and sand trucks, and give them plenty of room.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: What problems can wet brakes cause, according to subsection 2.13.2?
choice_a: Only reduced fuel economy
choice_b: Permanent brake failure requiring replacement
choice_c: Weak or uneven braking, wheel lockups, pulling to one side, or jackknife when pulling a trailer
choice_d: Only a warning light illuminating
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 states water in the brakes can cause weak or uneven application, grabbing, wheel lockups, pulling to one side, and jackknife if pulling a trailer.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: What should you do while crossing deep standing water, according to subsection 2.13.2's wet brakes guidance?
choice_a: Apply the brakes hard and hold them the entire crossing
choice_b: Shift into neutral and coast through
choice_c: Turn off the engine to prevent water damage
choice_d: Increase engine rpm and cross while keeping light pressure on the brakes
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 instructs increasing engine rpm and crossing the water while keeping light pressure on the brakes to keep the linings pressed against the drums.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: After driving through deep water, what should you do to verify your brakes are working properly?
choice_a: Check behind you, then make a test stop to see if the brakes work well
choice_b: Immediately resume normal highway speed
choice_c: Turn off the retarder permanently
choice_d: Apply maximum brake pressure while accelerating
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 advises making a test stop when safe, after checking behind you, to confirm brakes work well; if not, dry them out further.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: What caution does the manual give about applying brake pressure and accelerator together after crossing water?
choice_a: This is the required method and has no risk
choice_b: Don't apply too much brake pressure and accelerator at the same time, or you can overheat brake drums and linings
choice_c: It is only a concern in summer weather
choice_d: It only affects the parking brake
explanation: Subsection 2.13.2 cautions against applying too much brake pressure and accelerator simultaneously, since it can overheat brake drums and linings.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.13.2 - Driving

question: In very hot weather, how often does the manual recommend inspecting tires?
choice_a: Once per day
choice_b: Every 500 miles
choice_c: Every two hours or every 100 miles
choice_d: Only before starting the trip
explanation: Subsection 2.14.1 recommends inspecting tires every two hours or every 100 miles when driving in very hot weather.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: Should you let air out of a tire that has become hot in very hot weather, according to the manual?
choice_a: Yes, to bring pressure back to the cold rating
choice_b: Yes, but only by half the excess pressure
choice_c: Yes, if the tire feels warm to the touch
choice_d: No, or the pressure will be too low when the tires cool off
explanation: Subsection 2.14.1 states air pressure increases with temperature and warns not to let air out, or the pressure will be too low once the tires cool.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: What should you do if a tire is too hot to touch, per subsection 2.14.1?
choice_a: Remain stopped until the tire cools off
choice_b: Immediately let air out to cool it
choice_c: Continue driving at reduced speed
choice_d: Pour water directly on the tire
explanation: Subsection 2.14.1 instructs that if a tire is too hot to touch, you should remain stopped until it cools off, or the tire may blow out or catch fire.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: According to subsection 2.14.1, when is it probably safe to touch and open a radiator cap?
choice_a: Immediately after the engine is turned off
choice_b: When you can touch the radiator cap with your bare hand, meaning it is probably cool enough to open
choice_c: Only when the engine is still running
choice_d: Only using a thick cloth, regardless of temperature
explanation: Subsection 2.14.1 states if you can touch the radiator cap with your bare hand, it is probably cool enough to open.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: What is the first step when adding coolant to a system without a recovery or overflow tank, per subsection 2.14.1?
choice_a: Turn the cap directly to the fully open position
choice_b: Add coolant while the engine is running
choice_c: Shut the engine off
choice_d: Disconnect the battery
explanation: Subsection 2.14.1 lists shutting the engine off as the first step, followed by waiting until the engine has cooled before adding coolant.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: When removing a radiator cap from a pressurized system, what should you do after turning it slowly to the "first stop"?
choice_a: Remove it immediately
choice_b: Pour cold water on the radiator
choice_c: Turn it back to the closed position
choice_d: Step back while pressure is released from the cooling system
explanation: Subsection 2.14.1 instructs turning the cap slowly to the first stop to release the pressure seal, then stepping back while pressure is released.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: What problem can loose engine belts cause in very hot weather?
choice_a: The water pump and/or fan may not turn properly, resulting in overheating
choice_b: The transmission will shift too early
choice_c: The tires will wear unevenly
choice_d: The brakes will fade prematurely
explanation: Subsection 2.14.1 states loose belts will not turn the water pump and/or fan properly, resulting in overheating.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: What hazard does "bleeding tar" present in very hot weather, according to subsection 2.14.2?
choice_a: It damages tire tread permanently
choice_b: Spots where tar rises to the surface become very slippery
choice_c: It causes the engine to overheat
choice_d: It clogs the radiator
explanation: Subsection 2.14.2 warns that tar rising to the road surface in very hot weather creates spots that are very slippery.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.2 - Driving

question: Why does the manual advise going slowly enough to prevent overheating in very hot weather?
choice_a: To conserve fuel only
choice_b: Slower speeds are legally mandated above certain temperatures
choice_c: High speeds create more heat for tires and the engine, increasing chances of tire or engine failure
choice_d: To reduce engine noise
explanation: Subsection 2.14.2 explains high speeds create more heat for tires and the engine, which in desert conditions can increase the chance of tire failure, fire, or engine failure.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.2 - Driving

question: Why should you check coolant hoses for good condition before driving in hot weather?
choice_a: Hoses affect tire pressure readings
choice_b: Cracked hoses reduce fuel efficiency only
choice_c: Hoses are unrelated to engine cooling
choice_d: A broken hose while driving can lead to engine failure and even fire
explanation: Subsection 2.14.1 warns that a broken coolant hose while driving can lead to engine failure and even fire.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.14.1 - Vehicle Checks

question: What characterizes a "passive crossing" at a railroad-highway intersection?
choice_a: It has no traffic control device; the decision to stop or proceed rests entirely with the driver
choice_b: It has flashing lights but no gates
choice_c: It has gates, bells, and flashing lights
choice_d: It is only found on private roads
explanation: Subsection 2.15.1 defines a passive crossing as one without any traffic control device, where the driver alone must decide if there is sufficient clear space to cross safely.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.1 - Types of Crossings

question: Which of these is an example of an "active crossing" device described in subsection 2.15.1?
choice_a: A simple cross-buck sign with no lights
choice_b: Flashing red lights with bells and gates
choice_c: A speed limit sign
choice_d: A yield sign only
explanation: Subsection 2.15.1 describes active crossings as having devices such as flashing red lights (with or without bells) and flashing red lights with bells and gates.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.1 - Types of Crossings

question: What does the round, black-on-yellow advance warning sign at a railroad crossing tell you to do?
choice_a: Immediately apply your parking brake
choice_b: Sound your horn continuously
choice_c: Slow down, look and listen for the train, and be prepared to stop at the tracks
choice_d: Increase speed to clear the crossing quickly
explanation: Subsection 2.15.2 explains the round, black-on-yellow advance warning sign tells drivers to slow down, look and listen for the train, and be prepared to stop.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.2 - Warning Signs and Devices

question: If there is no white stop line painted on the pavement, how far from the nearest rail must a vehicle required to stop position itself?
choice_a: No closer than 5 feet or more than 25 feet
choice_b: Exactly at the rail
choice_c: No closer than 25 feet or more than 100 feet
choice_d: No closer than 15 feet or more than 50 feet from the nearest rail
explanation: Subsection 2.15.2 states vehicles required to stop, without a painted stop line, must stop no closer than 15 feet or more than 50 feet from the nearest rail of the nearest track.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.2 - Warning Signs and Devices

question: What must you do when the flashing red lights begin at a railroad crossing, according to subsection 2.15.2?
choice_a: Stop, because a train is approaching and you must yield the right-of-way
choice_b: Proceed cautiously without stopping
choice_c: Sound your horn and continue
choice_d: Only stop if you see the train itself
explanation: Subsection 2.15.2 states when flashing red lights begin, you must stop; a train is approaching and you are required to yield the right-of-way.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.2 - Warning Signs and Devices

question: When should you stop at a railroad crossing equipped with gates?
choice_a: Only after the gate has fully lowered
choice_b: When the lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers across the road lane
choice_c: Only when you hear the train horn
choice_d: Gates require no stop, only reduced speed
explanation: Subsection 2.15.2 instructs stopping when the lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers, then remaining stopped until the gates rise and lights stop flashing.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.2 - Warning Signs and Devices

question: What driving procedure does subsection 2.15.3 emphasize regarding trains at crossings?
choice_a: You may proceed if you believe you can beat the train
choice_b: Racing is acceptable if your vehicle is empty
choice_c: Never attempt to race a train to a crossing, since it's extremely difficult to judge a train's speed
choice_d: Only experienced drivers should attempt to race a train
explanation: Subsection 2.15.3 states you should never attempt to race a train to a crossing, since it is extremely difficult to judge the speed of an approaching train.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.3 - Driving Procedures

question: Why does subsection 2.15.3 warn "Don't Expect to Hear a Train"?
choice_a: Trains are required to sound horns at every crossing
choice_b: Train horns are inaudible beyond 10 feet
choice_c: All crossings are equipped with electronic warning speakers
choice_d: Trains may not, or are prohibited from, sounding horns approaching some crossings, and cab noise may prevent you from hearing it in time
explanation: Subsection 2.15.3 explains trains may be prohibited from sounding horns at some crossings, and cab noise may keep you from hearing the horn until the train is dangerously close.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.3 - Driving Procedures

question: Why must you "double check" at a double-track railroad crossing, per subsection 2.15.3?
choice_a: A train on one track may hide a train on the other track
choice_b: Double tracks always have malfunctioning signals
choice_c: Double-track crossings are only found in rural areas
choice_d: Trains on double tracks travel faster
explanation: Subsection 2.15.3 warns that a train on one track may hide a train on the other, so you must look both ways and be sure no other train is near before crossing.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.3 - Driving Procedures

question: According to subsection 2.15.4, when is a full stop required at a grade crossing?
choice_a: Only when a train is visible
choice_b: When the nature of the cargo makes a stop mandatory under state or federal regulations, or when otherwise required by law
choice_c: Only for buses, never for trucks
choice_d: Full stops are never required, only reduced speed
explanation: Subsection 2.15.4 states a full stop is required at grade crossings when cargo makes a stop mandatory under regulations, or when otherwise required by law.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.4 - Stopping Safely at Railroad-highway Crossings

question: According to subsection 2.15.5, about how long does it take a typical tractor-trailer unit to clear a single railroad track?
choice_a: 5 seconds
choice_b: 10 seconds
choice_c: At least 14 seconds
choice_d: 30 seconds
explanation: Subsection 2.15.5 states it takes a typical tractor-trailer unit at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds to clear a double track.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.5 - Crossing the Tracks

question: What does subsection 2.15.5 instruct about shifting gears while crossing railroad tracks?
choice_a: Shift to a higher gear for a faster crossing
choice_b: Shift to neutral to coast across
choice_c: Downshift immediately before the first rail
choice_d: Do not shift gears while crossing the tracks
explanation: Subsection 2.15.5 explicitly instructs drivers not to shift gears while crossing railroad tracks.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.5 - Crossing the Tracks

question: Which type of trailer does subsection 2.15.6 warn can get stuck on raised railroad crossings?
choice_a: Low slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, or possum-belly livestock trailers
choice_b: Standard flatbed trailers
choice_c: Refrigerated van trailers
choice_d: Tanker trailers exclusively
explanation: Subsection 2.15.6 warns that low slung units (lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock trailer) can get stuck on raised crossings.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.6 - Special Situations

question: If you get stuck on railroad tracks, what does the manual instruct you to do first?
choice_a: Try repeatedly to drive the vehicle off the tracks
choice_b: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks
choice_c: Stay in the vehicle and wait for the train
choice_d: Attempt to push the vehicle off the tracks yourself
explanation: Subsection 2.15.6 instructs that if you get stuck on the tracks, get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks immediately.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.6 - Special Situations

question: When calling for help after getting stuck on railroad tracks, what specific information should you give if posted?
choice_a: The train's estimated arrival time
choice_b: The crossing's construction date
choice_c: The DOT number, along with identifiable landmarks describing the crossing location
choice_d: The trailer's VIN number
explanation: Subsection 2.15.6 instructs giving the location using identifiable landmarks, especially the DOT number if posted, when calling 911 or another emergency number.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.6 - Special Situations

question: What does subsection 2.15.3 advise about relying solely on warning signals, gates, or flagmen?
choice_a: They are always 100% reliable and sufficient
choice_b: You may disregard other precautions if gates are present
choice_c: Only flagmen should be trusted, not automated signals
choice_d: You should not rely solely on them; be especially alert at crossings without gates or flashing lights
explanation: Subsection 2.15.3 ("Don't Rely on Signals") advises against relying solely on warning signals, gates, or flagmen, and to be especially alert where gates or flashing lights are absent.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.15.3 - Driving Procedures

question: According to subsection 2.16, what happens to your vehicle's speed on a long, steep downgrade due to gravity?
choice_a: Gravity causes the vehicle's speed to increase
choice_b: Gravity has no measurable effect on heavy vehicles
choice_c: Gravity only affects vehicles without trailers
choice_d: Gravity slows the vehicle automatically
explanation: Subsection 2.16 explains that in coming down long, steep downgrades, gravity causes the speed of your vehicle to increase.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16 - Mountain Driving

question: When should you shift into a low gear for a long downgrade, according to subsection 2.16.2?
choice_a: After your speed has already built up on the grade
choice_b: Before starting down the grade
choice_c: Only when the brakes begin to fade
choice_d: At the midpoint of the grade
explanation: Subsection 2.16.2 instructs shifting into a low gear before starting down the grade, warning that downshifting after speed has built up may not be possible.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.2 - Select the Right Gear before Starting Down the Grade

question: What primarily causes brakes to fade or fail on a long downgrade, according to subsection 2.16.3?
choice_a: Cold weather affecting brake fluid
choice_b: Using the engine braking effect too much
choice_c: Excessive heat from using the brakes too much instead of relying on engine braking
choice_d: Low tire pressure
explanation: Subsection 2.16.3 explains brakes can fade or fail from excessive heat caused by using them too much and not relying on the engine braking effect.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.3 - Brake Fading or Failure

question: In the manual's proper braking technique example with a 40 mph "safe" speed, at what speed should you release the brakes after applying them?
choice_a: 40 mph
choice_b: 30 mph
choice_c: 20 mph
choice_d: 35 mph (approximately five mph below the safe speed)
explanation: Subsection 2.16.4 gives the example of applying brakes at 40 mph and releasing them once speed drops to about 35 mph, five mph below the safe speed.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.4 - Proper Braking Technique

question: According to subsection 2.16.4, about how long should each brake application last using the proper braking technique?
choice_a: About three seconds
choice_b: About ten seconds
choice_c: About thirty seconds
choice_d: About one minute
explanation: Subsection 2.16.4 states the brake application should last for about three seconds when using the proper technique of reducing speed by 5 mph and releasing.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.4 - Proper Braking Technique

question: What are escape ramps designed to do, per subsection 2.16.4?
choice_a: Provide a shortcut to bypass mountain grades
choice_b: Stop runaway vehicles safely without injuring drivers and passengers, using a long bed of loose, soft material
choice_c: Allow vehicles to bypass weigh stations
choice_d: Serve as emergency fuel stations
explanation: Subsection 2.16.4 explains escape ramps use a long bed of loose, soft material (sometimes with an upgrade) to safely stop runaway vehicles without injuring occupants.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.4 - Proper Braking Technique

question: Which of the following is NOT listed among the factors for selecting a "safe" speed on a mountain grade in subsection 2.16.1?
choice_a: Total weight of the vehicle and cargo
choice_b: Steepness of the grade
choice_c: The color of the vehicle
choice_d: Road conditions and weather
explanation: Subsection 2.16.1 lists total weight, length and steepness of grade, road conditions, and weather as factors for selecting a safe speed; vehicle color is not a factor.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.1 - Select a "Safe" Speed

question: When is the braking effect of the engine greatest, according to subsection 2.16.1?
choice_a: When the transmission is in the highest gear
choice_b: When the engine is idling
choice_c: When the vehicle is coasting in neutral
choice_d: When the engine is near governed rpm and the transmission is in the lower gears
explanation: Subsection 2.16.1 states the braking effect of the engine is greatest when it is near the governed rpms and the transmission is in the lower gears.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.1 - Select a "Safe" Speed

question: Why might drivers of modern trucks need to use a lower gear going down a hill than the gear needed to climb it, per subsection 2.16.2?
choice_a: Modern trucks have low-friction parts, streamlined shapes, and more powerful engines, giving less resistance holding them back downhill
choice_b: Modern trucks have weaker brakes than older trucks
choice_c: Modern trucks cannot use engine braking at all
choice_d: It is only true for automatic transmissions
explanation: Subsection 2.16.2 explains new trucks' low friction parts, streamlined shapes, and more powerful engines mean less friction/drag holding them back going downhill, so a lower gear may be needed than for climbing.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.2 - Select the Right Gear before Starting Down the Grade

question: Why must brake adjustment be checked frequently, according to subsection 2.16.3?
choice_a: It is a one-time requirement set at manufacture
choice_b: Brakes can get out of adjustment quickly, especially with heavy use, and linings wear faster when hot
choice_c: Only annual inspections require checking adjustment
choice_d: Adjustment only matters for the parking brake
explanation: Subsection 2.16.3 explains brakes can get out of adjustment quickly with heavy use, and linings wear faster when hot, so brake adjustment must be checked frequently to avoid overheating and fade of remaining brakes.
source_note: New Jersey Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Subsection 2.16.3 - Brake Fading or Failure
